notes.meaning: God's people are called to bring heartfelt praise to the Lord. The phrase 'servants of the Lord' refers to all who belong to Him and worship Him faithfully. Repeating the call to praise shows that God's people should stir up their hearts with real joy and eagerness.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Latin translations read 'servants' as 'children,' which Augustine understood as a call to put away pride and approach God with child-like humility.

notes.meaning: Praising the Lord is not meant to stop after one moment or generation. God's character never changes, so His name is worthy of honour right now and through all time to come. Believers are called to keep honouring Him each day into eternity.

The Lord deserves praise across the whole world, from the far east where the sun comes up to the west where it goes down. His goodness touches every corner of the earth, so people everywhere have reason to give Him thanks. Our praise of Him should reach across all places and all hours of the day.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine understood this verse as a prophecy about the worldwide spread of the Church to all nations.

notes.meaning: The Lord rules high over every nation and empire on earth. While human rulers have limited land and short reigns, God's majesty reaches beyond the highest skies. Remembering His supreme greatness puts all earthly powers into proper perspective.

No king, angel, or false god compares to the true Lord. He sits on a heavenly throne that is higher than anything in the created universe. Knowing that our God is unmatched brings deep comfort and quiet confidence.

Even looking down at the heavens is an act of humility for God because He is so far above all things. Yet instead of remaining distant, He chooses to look closely at our world and care for human beings. His greatness is shown most clearly in how He stoops down to notice ordinary people.

The Lord takes special notice of those who are crushed, poor, and cast aside by society. Sitting in the dust or on a rubbish heap was an ancient picture of extreme poverty and loneliness. God does not overlook people in such misery, but reaches down to rescue them.

God does not simply pull the poor out of trouble; He grants them honour and a place among leaders. Scripture shows this happening in the lives of people like Joseph and David, who were raised from humble beginnings into positions of dignity. God delights to lift up the lowly and give them true worth among His people.

In ancient times, a childless woman often suffered harsh shame and felt insecure in her household. The Lord showed His power and tender care by giving children to women such as Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah, filling their homes with joy. The psalm ends with 'Hallelujah' because a God so high who cares so deeply for the hurting is worthy of all our praise.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw the joyful mother as a picture of the Church, which was once barren among the nations but grew into a fruitful spiritual mother to countless believers.
